_data.content: To be a successful restaurant employee, you should have understood that certain traits were needed.
My former restaurant employees should have been able to handle multiple orders from multiple tables simultaneously.
They had to handle these tasks  with efficiency and poise.
They had to take orders and deliver food to precise specifications.
They should have memorized the specials.

Express duty, advice, willingness, or intention to do something in spoken or written texts and in work and social contexts.

Understands extended speeches, lectures, articles and reports of the professional, academic, or daily life on a wide range of general and work topics, in conversations or presentations, spoken at a natural speed and in circumstances that make it more difficult to hear.
When + Present Perfect and If

You use when and if to talk about conditions that will be fulfilled before a situation can happen.

You use when with the Present Perfect to talk about a condition that needs to be completed before another one can occur.

You can also use when with the Present Perfect to suggest that something needs to happen before something else can happen. In that context, when has the meaning of as soon as, after, until.
Example: We'll get started when everyone has arrived.

You normally use if with the Present Simple in an if-clause to talk about a possible outcome. The outcome will be positive if the condition in the if-clause is fulfilled.
Example: We'll get better reviews if everyone works a little harder.
Look at the examples from the text:
Keep your interactions pleasant even when a customer has been unreasonable and rude.
If you are a bartender, server or a cook, you have to be able to accommodate your customer's demands and specifications.
If you are easily flustered, you will become overwhelmed.
If you don't consistently provide excellent service, you may diminish your restaurant's reputation.
When you have finished taking their order, you need to get table two more drinks.
You'll need to help up front, when they've left.
Modals for Duty or Obligation in the Past

You can use a variety of modals to talk about duties and obligations, to express what someone is responsible for and to give strong advice and recommendations.

You use should and have to to express duty and obligation in the past.
Let's look at the modals must, have to, have got to, and should.
You cannot use must to express duty or obligation in the past.

You use should + have + past participle to express duty in the past.
Example: You should have told me about your problems with the customers yesterday.

You use had to before verbs that talk about necessity. Had to implies that someone else imposed the necessity on you.
Example: You had to leave the kitchen completely clean before you left. = It implies that it was a duty to leave the kitchen clean, and it may not have been fulfilled.
Read the following examples from the text:
My former restaurant employees should have been able to handle multiple orders from multiple tables simultaneously, but they couldn't.
They should have memorized the specials.
You should have handled that in a delicate, friendly manner.
We had to provide that service in a friendly manner.
I had to order another round of drinks while grabbing more napkins.
